name: Bishop John Stephen Semeria, O.M.I.
office: First Oblate Vicar Apostolic of Jaffna
excerpt: The 14th of July was a remarkable day in the historical annals of the Diocese of Jaffna, as it remembered with gratitude the services of the first Oblate Bishop of the Apostolic Vicariate of Jaffna, Bishop John Stephen SEMERIA, as this year marks the 150th year of his heavenly birth.
body:
The 14th of July was a remarkable day in the historical annals of the Diocese of Jaffna, as it remembered with gratitude the services of the first Oblate Bishop of the Apostolic Vicariate of Jaffna, Bishop John Stephen SEMERIA, as this year marks the 150th year of his heavenly birth.

The day was made significant with two major events, namely the unveiling of a huge, beautiful statue of Bishop Semeria at the Cathedral and a memorial lecture on the bishop.

The installation of the statue began with a prayer conducted by the diocesan seminarians. The statue of the bishop was blessed and unveiled by Very Rev. Fr. P. J. Jebaratnam, the Vicar General of the diocese of Jaffna, together with the Oblate provincials of the Provinces of Jaffna and Colombo, Frs. Edwin VASANTHARAJAH and Irwin MORAES, and the provincial of the Holy Family Sisters of Bordeaux. There was a good number of people: Oblate Lay Associates, seminarians, Holy Family Sisters of Bordeaux, priests of the diocese of Jaffna and other religious.

The memorial lecture on Bishop Semeria took place at the nearby hall immediately after the installation of the statue. It began with prayer and a cultural welcome dance performed by members of MAMI. It was followed by the lighting of the traditional lamp and the garlanding of the picture of Bishop Semeria by Father Moraes. The Oblate Provincials and the Provincial of the Holy Family Sisters of Bordeaux addressed the gathering on the contribution of Bishop Semeria to the Church of Sri Lanka.

The climax was the memorial lecture on the 'Challenges Bishop Semeria encountered.' The lecture was delivered by Prof. Rev. Dr. S.V.B. Mangalarajah, Jaffna diocesan priest, senior lecturer at the Jaffna diocesan major seminary, who is a well-known historian in the country. He spoke of the challenges that the bishop faced with his predecessor, Bishop Orazio Betachini, the first Apostolic Vicar of the Vicariate, and with the Oratorian Missionaries who came from Goa, India, and looked after these lands for a long period of time before the Oblates. He spoke of Bishop Semeria’s capabilities as an administrator and how he met the challenges and situations of his day. The day’s programme came to an end with the Oblate anthem.

name: Archbishop Ernest Christopher Bonjean, O.M.I.
office: Vicar Apostolic of Jaffna & First Archbishop of Colombo
excerpt: Archbishop Ernest Christopher Bonjean, O.M.I., stands as one of the most visionary prelates in the history of the Catholic Church in Sri Lanka. Having arrived in Ceylon in 1856, he succeeded Bishop Stephen Semeria as Vicar Apostolic of Jaffna in 1868 and was subsequently elevated as the first Archbishop of the Metropolitan See of Colombo in 1886.
body:
Archbishop Ernest Christopher Bonjean, O.M.I., stands as one of the most visionary prelates in the history of the Catholic Church in Sri Lanka. Having arrived in Ceylon in 1856, he succeeded Bishop Stephen Semeria as Vicar Apostolic of Jaffna in 1868 and was subsequently elevated as the first Archbishop of the Metropolitan See of Colombo in 1886.

Archbishop Bonjean is revered as the father and chief architect of the Catholic denominational education system in Sri Lanka. Facing severe opposition from colonial educational policies, he forcefully advocated for state-assisted denominational schools that preserved religious identity while delivering high academic standards in both native vernacular languages (Tamil and Sinhala) and English.

In addition to his educational crusade, Archbishop Bonjean recognized the crucial role of Catholic journalism. He founded 'The Catholic Messenger' in Colombo and the 'Jaffna Catholic Guardian', establishing a powerful press apostolate to defend Catholic rights and promote literacy. He also laid the foundation stone for the magnificent St. Lucia's Cathedral in Kotahena, Colombo, and established St. Bernard's Major Seminary to foster native priestly vocations.

name: Archbishop Theophilus Andrew Melizan, O.M.I.
office: Bishop of Jaffna & Archbishop of Colombo
excerpt: Archbishop Andrew Melizan, O.M.I., served as Bishop of Jaffna from 1883 to 1893 and succeeded Archbishop Bonjean as Archbishop of Colombo from 1893 until his death in 1905. His episcopate was marked by dynamic expansion in secondary education and pastoral care.
body:
Archbishop Andrew Melizan, O.M.I., served as Bishop of Jaffna from 1883 to 1893 and succeeded Archbishop Bonjean as Archbishop of Colombo from 1893 until his death in 1905. His episcopate was marked by dynamic expansion in secondary education and pastoral care.

Under his visionary direction, St. Joseph's College in Colombo was founded in 1896, which quickly grew into one of the premier Catholic educational institutions in Asia. Similarly, in Jaffna, he significantly upgraded St. Patrick's College, establishing it as an epicenter of academic excellence and spiritual formation in Northern Sri Lanka.

Archbishop Melizan worked tirelessly to strengthen rural parishes, build mission chapels, and foster deep spiritual devotion among the faithful. His legacy is remembered through the numerous educational institutes and charitable societies he established across Ceylon.

name: Bishop Henry Joulain, O.M.I.
excerpt: Bishop Henry Joulain, O.M.I., guided the Diocese of Jaffna for twenty-six remarkable years (1893–1919). His tenure covered a period of significant growth and consolidation for the Church in Northern and Eastern Sri Lanka.
body:
Bishop Henry Joulain, O.M.I., guided the Diocese of Jaffna for twenty-six remarkable years (1893–1919). His tenure covered a period of significant growth and consolidation for the Church in Northern and Eastern Sri Lanka.

Bishop Joulain concentrated heavily on developing local indigenous clergy. He established St. Martin's Seminary in Jaffna to provide rigorous academic and spiritual formation for young Tamil seminarians. He also expanded primary schools in remote villages across the Mannar, Vanni, and Jaffna regions.

Known for his administrative prudence and deep fatherly care, Bishop Joulain constructed numerous churches, fostered pious sodalities, and maintained strong inter-community harmony until his peaceful passing in Jaffna in 1919.

name: Bishop Jules-Joseph Brault, O.M.I.
excerpt: Bishop Jules Brault, O.M.I., served as Bishop of Jaffna from 1919 to 1923. Though his episcopal ministry was cut short by his early death, his profound spiritual leadership left a lasting mark on the diocese.
body:
Bishop Jules Brault, O.M.I., served as Bishop of Jaffna from 1919 to 1923. Though his episcopal ministry was cut short by his early death, his profound spiritual leadership left a lasting mark on the diocese.

Ascending to the episcopate in the aftermath of World War I, Bishop Brault focused on post-war spiritual renewal, organizing diocesan missions, strengthening catechetical teaching in parishes, and providing relief to rural communities suffering from economic hardships.

He was remembered by the clergy and laity of Jaffna as a shepherd of humble prayer, deep Marian devotion, and tireless dedication to the welfare of the poor.

name: Archbishop Antony Coudert, O.M.I.
excerpt: Archbishop Antony Coudert, O.M.I., served the Archdiocese of Colombo for over two decades (1905–1929), guiding the Western Archdiocese through crucial years of growth and institutional maturity.
body:
Archbishop Antony Coudert, O.M.I., served the Archdiocese of Colombo for over two decades (1905–1929), guiding the Western Archdiocese through crucial years of growth and institutional maturity.

Archbishop Coudert prioritized Catholic education, establishing parish schools throughout the Western Province and supporting higher education institutions. He completed major structural works on St. Lucia's Cathedral and consecrated numerous new parish churches.

His episcopate was characterized by strong administrative governance, warm encouragement of lay apostolates, and the expansion of healthcare and orphanages managed by religious congregations.

name: Archbishop Pierre-Jean Marque, O.M.I.
excerpt: Archbishop Peter Marque, O.M.I., served as Archbishop of Colombo from 1929 to 1937, leaving an indelible mark on Catholic higher education and social apostolates.
body:
Archbishop Peter Marque, O.M.I., served as Archbishop of Colombo from 1929 to 1937, leaving an indelible mark on Catholic higher education and social apostolates.

A visionary educator, Archbishop Marque founded Aquinas University College in Colombo to afford Catholic youth the opportunity for tertiary education steeped in Christian ethics. He was deeply attentive to social justice, encouraging Catholic trade unions, workers' relief funds, and organized charity during the difficult Great Depression era.

He also actively promoted indigenous vocations, ensuring that local Sri Lankan priests were appointed to key administrative and educational posts within the Archdiocese.

name: Mgr. Aloysius M. Perera
office: Vicar General & Indigenous Prelate of Colombo
excerpt: Monsignor Aloysius M. Perera was a distinguished Sri Lankan prelate born in Kotahena, Colombo. He represented a vital generation of native clergy who assumed major administrative responsibilities in the Church.
body:
Monsignor Aloysius M. Perera was a distinguished Sri Lankan prelate born in Kotahena, Colombo. He represented a vital generation of native clergy who assumed major administrative responsibilities in the Church.

Serving as Vicar General of the Archdiocese of Colombo, Mgr. Perera bridged the transition between European missionary leadership and the emerging indigenous hierarchy. He was highly esteemed for his pastoral empathy, eloquent preaching, and untiring care for urban working-class parishes in Colombo.

name: Archbishop Jean-Marie Masson, O.M.I.
excerpt: Archbishop Jean-Marie Masson, O.M.I., guided the Archdiocese of Colombo through the perilous years of World War II (1938–1947).
body:
Archbishop Jean-Marie Masson, O.M.I., guided the Archdiocese of Colombo through the perilous years of World War II (1938–1947).

During the height of World War II in 1940, as Sri Lanka faced potential military bombardment, Archbishop Masson made a solemn vow to build a National Basilica dedicated to Our Lady of Lanka if the island was spared from destruction. Following the island's protection, he initiated the construction of the magnificent Basilica of Our Lady of Lanka in Tewatte, Ragama.

Archbishop Masson was also a strong proponent of inculturation and paved the way for the appointment of the first native Sri Lankan Archbishop.

name: Bishop Alfred Guyomar, O.M.I.
excerpt: Bishop Alfred Guyomar, O.M.I., served as Bishop of Jaffna for a quarter-century (1924–1950), administering a vast diocese that encompassed Northern and Eastern Sri Lanka.
body:
Bishop Alfred Guyomar, O.M.I., served as Bishop of Jaffna for a quarter-century (1924–1950), administering a vast diocese that encompassed Northern and Eastern Sri Lanka.

A scholar holding doctorates in theology and science, Bishop Guyomar dedicated his episcopate to expanding educational facilities, founding secondary schools in Batticaloa, Trincomalee, and Mannar. He nurtured local Catholic literature, supported agricultural cooperatives in the Vanni, and fortified parish communities until his retirement in 1950.

name: Bishop Jerome Emilianus Pillai, O.M.I.
office: First Indigenous Tamil Bishop of Jaffna
excerpt: Bishop Jerome Emilianus Pillai, O.M.I., made history when he was consecrated in 1950 as the first indigenous Sri Lankan Tamil Bishop of the Diocese of Jaffna (1950–1972).
body:
Bishop Jerome Emilianus Pillai, O.M.I., made history when he was consecrated in 1950 as the first indigenous Sri Lankan Tamil Bishop of the Diocese of Jaffna (1950–1972).

Bishop Pillai was an eminent scholar, linguist, and educator who championed the introduction of vernacular Tamil in the sacred liturgy following the Second Vatican Council. He translated liturgical texts, authored theological works in Tamil, and established Catholic cultural institutions.

During times of political and national tension, Bishop Pillai stood as a courageous defender of human rights, linguistic equity, and social justice for minority communities in Sri Lanka.

name: Thomas Cardinal Cooray, O.M.I.
office: First Sri Lankan Cardinal & Archbishop of Colombo
excerpt: His Eminence Thomas Cardinal Cooray, O.M.I., was a monumental figure in Sri Lankan history, serving as Archbishop of Colombo (1947–1976) and becoming the first Sri Lankan elevated to the Sacred College of Cardinals by Pope Paul VI in 1965.
body:
His Eminence Thomas Cardinal Cooray, O.M.I., was a monumental figure in Sri Lankan history, serving as Archbishop of Colombo (1947–1976) and becoming the first Sri Lankan elevated to the Sacred College of Cardinals by Pope Paul VI in 1965.

Cardinal Cooray fulfilled the war-time vow of his predecessor by completing the construction of the National Basilica of Our Lady of Lanka at Tewatte, Ragama. He actively participated in the Second Vatican Council (1962–1965) and masterminded the post-conciliar renewal across Sri Lanka, promoting indigenous music, Sinhala liturgy, and lay ministry.

A statesman of immense spiritual dignity, he navigated the nationalization of schools in 1960 with wisdom, preserving Catholic education through private non-fee-levying schools. His cause for beatification is currently underway.

name: Bishop Edmund Peiris, O.M.I.
excerpt: Bishop Edmund Peiris, O.M.I., was consecrated in 1940 as the first Bishop of the newly created Diocese of Chilaw (1940–1972).
body:
Bishop Edmund Peiris, O.M.I., was consecrated in 1940 as the first Bishop of the newly created Diocese of Chilaw (1940–1972).

A internationally respected historian, oriental scholar, and musicologist, Bishop Peiris pioneered the inculturation of Catholic liturgy in Sri Lanka. He researched ancient Sinhala passion plays (Pasku), traditional carols (Kantharu), and sacred hymns, integrating indigenous cultural forms into Catholic worship.

He authored foundational historical volumes on the Church in Sri Lanka and established vibrant educational and agricultural institutions throughout the Wayamba region.

name: Bishop Henry Joy Goonewardene, O.M.I.
excerpt: Bishop Henry Joy Goonewardene, O.M.I., served with heroic missionary zeal as the Bishop of Anuradhapura in the North Central Province.
body:
Bishop Henry Joy Goonewardene, O.M.I., served with heroic missionary zeal as the Bishop of Anuradhapura in the North Central Province.

Serving in a predominantly Buddhist heartland, Bishop Goonewardene focused on inter-religious dialogue, social development, and rural upliftment. He established clean water projects, farming collectives, and youth vocational centers, embodying Christ's love through compassionate service to all communities.

name: Bishop Edmund J. Fernando, O.M.I.
office: Bishop of Badulla & Auxiliary Bishop of Colombo
excerpt: Bishop Edmund J. Fernando, O.M.I., served as Auxiliary Bishop of Colombo and subsequently as Bishop of Badulla (1979–1997) in the Uva Province.
body:
Bishop Edmund J. Fernando, O.M.I., served as Auxiliary Bishop of Colombo and subsequently as Bishop of Badulla (1979–1997) in the Uva Province.

Bishop Fernando dedicated his episcopate to ministering among impoverished plantation workers and rural estate communities in the hill country. He expanded catechetical training, built rural clinics, and advocated for the civic and human rights of estate Tamil workers.

name: Bishop Victor Gnanapragasam, O.M.I.
office: Bishop & Vicar Apostolic of Quetta, Pakistan
excerpt: Bishop Victor Gnanapragasam, O.M.I., born in Passaiyoor, Jaffna, represents the global missionary spirit of the Sri Lankan Oblates.
body:
Bishop Victor Gnanapragasam, O.M.I., born in Passaiyoor, Jaffna, represents the global missionary spirit of the Sri Lankan Oblates.

After serving in Sri Lanka, he volunteered for foreign missions in Pakistan in 1989. In 2002, Pope John Paul II appointed him the first Apostolic Prefect of Quetta, Balochistan, and in 2010 he was consecrated Bishop as the first Vicar Apostolic of Quetta.

In a challenging mission field, Bishop Victor built schools, hostel facilities for needy students, and promoted inter-faith dialogue between Christians and Muslims until his heavenly birth in Quetta in December 2020.
